editorialDecl.p: New English translation produced by the Falsafa project (Thothica) using an in-house agentic AI translation system, rendered from the Perseus source edition and reviewed by the project. Contributed to provide a translation for a work that previously had no English translation in the corpus.

div.p: Do just this, my Lucilius: lay claim to yourself for yourself, and the time that until now was either being taken from you, or filched, or slipping away, gather up and keep. Convince yourself that what I write is the truth: some of our hours are torn from us, some quietly withdrawn, some simply run off. Yet the most shameful loss is the one that comes through carelessness. And if you care to notice, the greatest part of life passes while we are doing wrong, a great part while we are doing nothing, the whole of life while we are doing something other than we should.

From what you write to me, and from what I hear, I conceive good hope of you: you do not run about, nor unsettle yourself by changes of place. Such tossing to and fro is the mark of a sick mind. The first proof of a well-ordered mind, I think, is to be able to halt and to abide with oneself.

You handed letters to be brought to me, as you write, to a friend of yours; then you warn me not to share with him all that concerns you, since you yourself are not in the habit of doing so: thus in one and the same letter you have both called him a friend and denied it. And so, if you used that word in a general sense, as we call all candidates "good men," as we greet passers-by, when their name does not come to mind, by the title of "master," let it pass.

Persevere as you have begun, and hasten as much as you can, that you may the longer enjoy a mind corrected and set in order. You enjoy it, indeed, even while you are correcting it, even while you are setting it in order; yet that other pleasure is of a different kind which is gathered from the contemplation of a mind pure and shining and free from every stain.

That you study so stubbornly and, laying all else aside, pursue this one thing, that you make yourself better day by day, I both approve and rejoice; and I not only urge you to persevere, but even beg you to do so. But this I warn you: do not, after the fashion of those who desire not to make progress but to be noticed, do anything in your dress or manner of life that would be conspicuous.

I perceive, Lucilius, that I am not merely being corrected but transformed. Nor do I now promise or hope that there is nothing left in me that needs changing. How should I not have many things that ought to be gathered in, thinned down, raised up? And this very thing is a proof of a mind changed for the better, that it sees its own faults, which until now it did not know. To certain sick men congratulation is offered when they themselves have felt that they are sick.

You ask what you think you should chiefly avoid? The crowd. You cannot yet be trusted to it in safety. I at least will confess my own weakness: I never bring back the character I took out. Something of what I had composed is thrown into disorder; something of what I had driven off returns. What happens to the sick, whom a long weakness has so affected that they cannot be brought out anywhere without harm, this happens to us, whose minds are recovering from a long sickness.

"Do you," you say, "bid me avoid the crowd, withdraw, and be content with my own conscience? Where are those precepts of your school, which command us to die in action?" As for that—that I seem to you for the present to be counselling inaction—it is for this that I have shut myself away and barred the doors, that I might be able to help the greater number. No day passes for me in idleness. I claim part of the nights for my studies. I do not give myself to sleep, but yield to it, and hold my eyes, wearied and sinking with watching, to their task.

You desire to know whether Epicurus is right when, in a certain letter, he blames those who say that the wise man is content with himself and for that reason has no need of a friend. This is the charge Epicurus brings against Stilbo and those to whom the highest good seemed to be a mind incapable of feeling.

So it is, I do not change my opinion: flee the multitude, flee the few, flee even a single companion. I have no one with whom I should wish you shared. And see what an opinion of you I hold: I dare to entrust you to yourself. Crates, as they say, the pupil of this very Stilbo whom I mentioned in my last letter, when he had seen a young man walking apart by himself, asked what he was doing there alone. "I am talking with myself," he said. To which Crates replied: "Take care, I beg you, and pay close heed; you are talking with a bad man."

You write that you have read most eagerly the books of Fabianus Papirius which are entitled 'On Civil Affairs,' and that they have not answered your expectation; then, forgetting that it is a philosopher who is in question, you find fault with his style. Suppose it is as you say, and that the words pour out and are not driven home; in the first place that has its own charm, and there is a comeliness proper to a discourse that glides gently. For I think it makes a great difference whether it has fallen out or flowed. Add now this difference too, which I am about to mention. Fabianus seems to me not to let his words fall, but to pour them out; they are so copious that they are sent forth without disorder, yet move with a certain order.

Every day, every hour shows us how mere a nothing we are, and warns by some fresh proof those who have forgotten their frailty; and then, while we are dreaming of things eternal, it forces us to look toward death. Do you ask what this opening is meant to convey? You knew Cornelius Senecio, a Roman knight of distinction and obliging temper: from humble beginnings he had pushed himself forward, and already his course toward the rest lay downhill. For rank grows more easily than it begins.

Just as a man who rouses one who is enjoying a pleasant dream is a nuisance, since he takes away a pleasure that, though false, still produces the effect of a true one, so your letter has done me an injury. For it called me back when I had surrendered myself to a congenial meditation and would have gone further, had I been allowed.

Why do you look about you at those things which can perhaps befall you, but can also fail to befall? I mean fire, collapse, and the rest, which happen to us without lying in wait for us; look rather at those, avoid those, which watch us and lie in ambush for us. Rarer are the mishaps, even if grave, of being shipwrecked or of being thrown from one's carriage; from man to man the danger is a daily one. Against this prepare yourself, this gaze upon with intent eyes. There is no evil more frequent, none more persistent, none more insinuating.

I have fled to my villa at Nomentum, to escape what, do you suppose? The city? No, a fever, and one that was creeping up on me. It had already laid its hand upon me. The physician said it was the beginnings, since my pulse was disordered and irregular and disturbing its natural measure. And so I ordered a carriage to be made ready at once; though my Paulina held me back, I persisted in going out; I had on my lips the saying of my master Gallio, who, when he had begun to have a fever in Achaia, immediately went aboard ship, crying out that the sickness belonged not to his body but to the place.

I will tell you what you must observe, that you may live more safely. Yet I think you should listen to these precepts as if I were teaching you by what method you should keep good health on your estate at Ardea. Consider what the things are that goad a man to the destruction of a man: you will find hope, envy, hatred, fear, contempt.

I answer your letters rather late, not because I am hard pressed by business. Beware of accepting that excuse; I am at leisure, and all are at leisure who wish to be. No affairs pursue a man. Men themselves embrace them and think busyness to be a proof of happiness. What, then, was the reason why I did not answer at once? The matter you were inquiring about was coming up in the framework of my own work.

Where is that prudence of yours? Where your subtlety in discerning things? Where your greatness of soul? Does so trifling a matter already vex you? Your slaves thought your busyness an opportunity for flight. If friends were deceiving you—for let them by all means keep the name which our error has imposed on them, and be called by it, that they may be no more disgraceful—then something would be lacking in all your affairs; as it is, those are lacking who were both wasting your effort and believing you to be a nuisance to others.

What you ask about is one of those things which it concerns one to know only for the sake of knowing. But none the less, because it does concern you, you are in haste and unwilling to wait for the books which at this very moment I am arranging, containing the whole moral part of philosophy. I will dispatch it at once; yet I will first write how this craving for learning, with which I see you burning, should be ordered, lest it impede its own self.

You wish to know whether a wise man can profit a wise man. We say that the wise man is full of every good and has attained the highest things; how, then, anyone can profit one who possesses the highest good is the question. Good men profit one another; for they exercise their virtues and keep wisdom in its own condition. Each requires someone with whom to compare notes, with whom to inquire.

Your friend, a youth of good natural parts, has talked with me; and his first conversation showed how much spirit, how much talent, and how much progress too there was already in him. He gave us a foretaste, to which he will live up. For he spoke not from preparation, but caught off his guard. When he was collecting himself, he could scarcely shake off his bashfulness—a good sign in a young man; so deeply did the blush spread over him from within. This, so far as I suspect, will attend him even when he has steadied himself and stripped off all his faults—will attend him even when he is wise. For no wisdom drives off the natural defects of the body; what is implanted and inborn may be softened by practice, but not overcome.

From my villa at Nomentum I send you greeting, and bid you have a good mind, that is, the gods all propitious, whom that man has appeased and favourable who has made himself propitious to himself. Set aside for the present the view that pleases certain people, that to each of us a god is given as a tutor, not indeed of the regular order, but one of a lower rank, of the number of those whom Ovid calls "the gods of the commons." Yet I would have you set this aside in such a way as to remember that our ancestors, who believed it, were Stoics; for they gave to each man both a Genius and a Juno.

You have asked me what sophismata are called in Latin. Many have tried to impose a name upon them, but none has stuck; evidently, because the thing itself was not received among us, nor in use, the name too was resisted. Yet the term that Cicero used seems to me most apt: he calls them cavillationes, quibbles.

I desire, by Hercules, that your friend be moulded, as you wish, and trained; but he is caught when very hard, or rather, what is more troublesome, he is caught when very soft and broken by a long and evil habit. Let me give you an illustration from our own craft.

You wish me to write to you what I think of this question that is bandied about among our school: whether justice, courage, prudence, and the other virtues are living creatures. By this subtlety, dearest Lucilius, we have brought it about that we seem to exercise our wits among trifles and to waste our leisure on disputations that will profit nothing. I will do what you wish, and will set forth what our school thinks. But I declare that I am of another opinion: I think there are certain things that befit a man in Greek slippers and Greek cloak. So let me tell you what it is that moved the ancients, or what the ancients have moved.

You ask why, at certain periods, a style of corrupt character has come forth, and how minds have come to incline toward certain faults, so that at one time an inflated manner of exposition flourished, at another a broken one drawn out into the fashion of a song? Why at one time bold sentiments that overstepped belief gave pleasure, at another abrupt and pregnant epigrams, in which more had to be understood than was heard? Why there was an age which used the right of metaphor without shame? The reason is what you commonly hear, what among the Greeks passed into a proverb: as a man's life, so was his speech.

I would not have you too anxious about words and composition, my dear Lucilius; I have greater things for you to care about. Ask what you are to write, not how; and even this, not that you may write it, but that you may feel it, that those things you have felt you may the more apply to yourself and, as it were, set your seal upon them. Whosoever's speech you see to be over-careful and polished, know that his mind too is no less taken up with petty things.

Whether it is better to have moderate passions or none has often been inquired. Our school drive them out, the Peripatetics moderate them. I do not see how any moderate amount of a disease can be wholesome or useful. Do not be afraid; I take from you none of the things you do not wish to be denied. I will show myself easy and indulgent toward the things you cling to and think either necessary to life or useful or pleasant; I will only take away the fault. For when I have forbidden you to crave, I will permit you to wish, that you may do those very same things undismayed, with a surer counsel, that you may feel pleasures themselves more keenly; why should they not come to you the more, if you command them rather than serve them?

You will contrive much trouble for me and, while you know it not, will thrust me into a great quarrel and vexation, you who set me such little questions, in which I can neither dissent from our school without loss of their goodwill, nor agree with them without loss of my conscience. You ask whether it is true, what the Stoics hold, that wisdom is a good, but to be wise is not a good. First I will set forth what the Stoics think; then I will venture to give my own opinion.

You demand of me more frequent letters. Let us compare accounts; you will not be able to pay. It had indeed been agreed that yours should come first, that you should write, and I should answer. But I will not be difficult; I know you can be trusted on credit. And so I will give in advance, and will not do what Cicero, that most eloquent man, bids Atticus do, that even if he has no matter to write of, he should write whatever comes to his lips.

Whenever I have discovered something, I do not wait until you say, "into the common stock." I say it to myself. You ask what it is that I have discovered; open your lap, it is pure gain. I will teach you how you may become rich most quickly. How keenly you long to hear! And not without reason; I will lead you by a short cut to the greatest riches. Yet you will need a creditor; that you may do business, you must run into debt, but I would not have you borrow through a go-between, I would not have the brokers bandy your name about.

Wherever I turn, I see the proofs of my old age. I had come to my place in the suburbs and was complaining of the expense of the building, which was falling to ruin. The steward told me it was no fault of his own neglect—he was doing everything—but the house was old. This house grew up under my own hands; what is to become of me, if stones of my own age are so crumbling?

Your letter has wandered through several little questions, but has settled upon one, and desires this to be cleared up: how the notion of the good and the honourable has come to us. These two are, with others, distinct things; with us they are only divided.

You will quarrel with me, I see, when I have set forth to you today's little question, in which we have stuck long enough. For again you will exclaim: "What has this to do with morals?" But exclaim away, while I first set against you others with whom to quarrel, Posidonius and Archidemus; these shall stand trial. Then I will say: not whatever is moral makes good morals.

The day has now felt its loss. It has rebounded somewhat, yet so that there is still a liberal space, if a man rises with the day itself, so to speak. He is more dutiful and better who awaits the day and catches the first light; base is he who lies half-asleep when the sun is high, whose waking begins at midday; and to many even this is before dawn.

Worn out by a journey troublesome rather than long, I reached my villa at Alba late at night; I have nothing ready except myself. And so I lay aside my weariness on the little couch, and make the best of this delay of cook and baker. For I talk with myself about this very thing, how nothing is grievous which you take lightly, how there is nothing to be indignant at unless you yourself build it up by being indignant.

"Many precepts of the ancients I could relate to you, unless you shrink back and are loth to learn these slight cares." But you do not shrink back, nor does any subtlety drive you off. It is not the mark of your refinement to pursue only the great and the easy. I approve this, that you reduce all things to some progress, and are offended only then, when by the utmost subtlety nothing is accomplished. That this shall not happen even now, I will take pains. The question is, whether the good is grasped by sense or by intellect. To this is joined the point that it is not present in dumb animals and in infants.

I know that you have much spirit. For even before you had armed yourself with wholesome precepts that overcome hardships, you were sufficiently pleased with yourself against fortune; and much more so after you came to grips with her and tested your strength—a strength that can never give a sure confidence in itself, except when many difficulties have appeared on this side and on that, and sometimes indeed have drawn nearer. Thus is that true spirit proved, which will not pass under another's control.

I confess that an affection for our own body is implanted in us; I confess that we have the care of it. I do not deny that it should be indulged; I deny that it should be served. For the man who serves his body will serve many masters—the man who fears overmuch for it, who refers everything to it.

There was an old custom, kept down to my own time, of adding at the beginning of a letter: "If you are well, it is well; I am well." We do rightly to say: "If you are practising philosophy, it is well." For this at last is to be well. Without this the mind is sick. The body too, even if it has great strength, is sound only in the way a madman or a frenzied man is sound.

It is clear to you, Lucilius, I know, that no one can live happily, nor even tolerably, without the pursuit of wisdom; and that the happy life is brought about by perfected wisdom, but a tolerable one even by wisdom begun. But this, which is clear, must be made firm and driven deeper by daily meditation; there is more labour in keeping your resolutions than in resolving upon what is honourable. You must persevere and add strength by unremitting study, until that which is good will becomes a good disposition of mind.

Cast away all these things, if you are wise—nay, that you may be wise—and strive toward a sound mind with all speed and all your strength. If there is anything that holds you back, either disentangle yourself from it or cut it away. "My estate," you say, "delays me; I wish to arrange it so that it may suffice for a man doing nothing, lest poverty be a burden to me, or I to anyone."

It is December, the month when the city is at its busiest sweat. License has been given to public extravagance. Everything resounds with vast preparations, as though there were any difference between the Saturnalia and the days of doing business. So little difference is there, that he seems to me not to have been wrong who said December once was a month, but now is a year.

I leap for joy as often as I receive your letters. For they fill me with good hope, and now they no longer promise concerning you, but pledge. So do, I pray and beseech you. For what better thing have I to ask of a friend than what I am about to ask for his own sake? If you can, withdraw yourself from those occupations; if not, tear yourself away. We have scattered time enough; let us begin, in old age, to gather in our gear.

If you are well, and think yourself worthy at some time to become your own, I rejoice. For it will be my glory if I draw you out of that place where you toss about with no hope of escape. But this, my Lucilius, I beg and exhort you: let philosophy down into the deepest part of your breast, and take the proof of your progress not from speech nor from writing, but from firmness of mind and the diminishing of desires; prove your words by deeds.

Do you judge that your business is with those men of whom you had written? Your greatest business is with yourself; you are a trouble to yourself. You do not know what you want; you approve the honourable better than you pursue it; you see where happiness is placed, but you dare not come to it. And what it is that hinders you, since you yourself discern it too little, I will tell you. You judge these things to be great which you are about to leave, and, when you have set before yourself that security to which you are to pass over, the glitter of this life from which you are about to withdraw holds you fast, as though you were about to fall into things squalid and obscure.

You now understand that you must be drawn out of those occupations that are showy and evil. But how you may achieve this, you ask. Certain things are pointed out only by one who is present. The physician cannot by letters choose the right time for food or for the bath; the pulse must be felt. There is an old proverb that the gladiator takes his counsel in the arena; something in the adversary's face, something in his moving hand, something in the very inclination of his body, warns the watcher.

Do you suppose I am going to write to you how kindly the winter has dealt with us—a winter both mild and short—how grudging the spring is, how perverse its cold, and other such trifles of those who hunt for something to say? No, I will write something that may profit both me and you. And what will that be, except that I exhort you to a sound mind? Do you ask what the foundation of this is? That you should not rejoice in vain things. I said it was the foundation; it is the very crown.

You write that you are anxious about the outcome of a lawsuit which an enemy's fury threatens you with, and you suppose that I will counsel you to set before yourself better things and to rest in a flattering hope. For what need is there to summon up evils, soon enough to be borne when they come, to anticipate them, and to lose the present time through fear of the future? It is, without doubt, foolish, because you are at some time to be wretched, to be wretched already. But I will lead you to security by another road.

As regards our two friends, we must go by different roads; the faults of the one must be corrected, those of the other broken. I will use my full freedom. I do not love him unless I give offence. "What then?" you say. "Do you think to keep a forty-year-old ward under your guardianship? Consider his age, now hard and intractable. He cannot be reshaped; only tender things are moulded."

Only a moment ago I was telling you that old age was within my sight; now I am afraid I have left old age behind me. Some other word fits these years of mine, and certainly this body, for old age is the name of a weary age, not a broken one: count me among the decrepit, among those who are touching the very end.

"You," you say, "give me advice? For have you already advised yourself, already set yourself right? Is that why you have time to spare for mending others?" I am not so shameless as to undertake cures while I am sick; rather, as though I lay in the same hospital ward, I talk with you about the malady we share and pass on the remedies. So then, listen to me as though I were speaking to myself. I admit you to my private chamber, and with you for witness I call myself to account.

Do you think this has befallen you alone, and do you marvel at it as at some strange thing, that with travel so long and so many changes of scene you have not shaken off the gloom and heaviness of your mind? You must change the mind, not the sky. Though you cross the wide sea, though, as our Virgil says, "lands and cities fall away," your faults will follow you wherever you go.

You ask about our friend Marcellinus and wish to know how he fares. He comes to us seldom, for no other reason than that he is afraid to hear the truth, a danger from which he is now far removed. For one must speak only to him who will listen. Hence about Diogenes, and no less about the other Cynics, who made indiscriminate use of their freedom and admonished all they met, it is usually doubted whether they ought to have done so.

I have seen Aufidius Bassus, that most excellent man, shattered and wrestling with his age. But by now it weighs him down more than he can be lifted up; old age has settled upon him with its full and total weight. You know that he was always of a feeble and exhausted body. For a long time he held it together, or, to speak more truly, kept it going; suddenly it has failed.

I recognize my Lucilius; he is beginning to show the man he promised to be. Follow that impulse of the mind by which you were making for all that is best, trampling on the goods that the crowd prizes. I do not wish you to become greater and better than you were striving to be. Your foundations have taken up much ground; only accomplish as much as you set out to do, and work over those things you carried with you in your mind.

I make inquiry about you and question everyone who comes from that region of yours: what you are doing, where and with whom you are passing your time. You cannot deceive me; I am with you. Live in such a way as though I were to hear of whatever you do, nay, as though I were to see it. Do you ask what most delights me among the things I hear about you? That I hear nothing, that most of those whom I question do not know what you are doing.

You desire that to these letters, as to the earlier ones, some sayings of our great men be added. They were not occupied with little flowers; their whole texture is manly. Know that there is unevenness wherever the parts that stand out are conspicuous. A single tree is no object of wonder where the whole forest has risen to the same height.

I grow and exult and, shaking off my old age, kindle anew, as often as I understand from the things you do and write how far you have outstripped yourself—for the crowd you left behind long ago. If the tree he has brought to fruit delights the farmer, if the shepherd takes pleasure in the increase of his flock, if no one regards his foster-child otherwise than as judging the youth's coming of age his own, what do you suppose befalls those who have reared minds and who suddenly see what they shaped tender now full-grown?

When I beg you so urgently to apply yourself to study, I am attending to my own business; I wish to have you for a friend, and this cannot fall to me unless you go on to cultivate yourself as you have begun. For now you love me, but you are not my friend. "What then? Are these things different from each other?" Nay, they are unlike. He who is a friend loves; he who loves is not necessarily a friend. Therefore friendship is always profitable, but love sometimes even does harm. If for nothing else, make progress at least for this, that you may learn to love.

Encourage your friend to despise with a great spirit those who reproach him because he has sought obscurity and leisure, because he has resigned his rank, and because, when he might have attained more, he has preferred peace to all else. Let him show them daily how usefully he has managed his own affairs. Those who are envied will not cease to pass on; some will be crushed, others will fall. Prosperity is a restless thing; it harasses itself. It troubles the brain in more than one way; it goads different men to different ends, some toward power, others toward extravagance. It puffs up some, it softens others and wholly dissolves them.

The strongest bond there is to a good mind—you have promised to be a good man, you have been bound by the oath. Anyone will laugh at you who tells you that the soldier's service is soft and easy. I do not wish you to be deceived. The words of this most honourable enlistment and of that most shameful one are the same: "to be burned, to be bound, and to be slain by the sword."

You are right to demand that we make this exchange of letters between us a frequent one. Conversation does the most good, because it creeps into the mind little by little. Discourses prepared beforehand and poured out before a listening crowd have more noise, less intimacy. Philosophy is good counsel; and no one gives counsel at the top of his voice. Sometimes one must use even those harangues, so to speak, where the man who hesitates must be driven on; but where the aim is not that he should wish to learn, but that he should learn, one must come down to these quieter words. They enter more easily and take hold; for one needs not many words, but effective ones.

The notebooks you ask for, carefully arranged and compressed into small compass, I will indeed put together. But consider whether the method in due order may not be more profitable than this thing which is now commonly called a breviary, and was once, when men spoke Latin, called a summary. The former is more necessary to one who is learning, the latter to one who already knows. For the one teaches, the other reminds. But I shall furnish you abundance of both. From me there is no reason for you to demand this or that authority: he who gives a sponsor is himself unknown.

I thank you for writing to me so often. For in the one way you can, you show yourself to me. Never do I receive a letter of yours but at once we are together. If portraits of absent friends are pleasant to us, which renew the memory and ease our longing with a false and empty comfort, how much more pleasant are letters, which bring the true traces, the true marks of an absent friend? For that which is sweetest in the sight of a friend, the hand impressed upon the letter affords: recognition.

You are doing an excellent thing, and one wholesome for yourself, if, as you write, you persevere in going toward a good mind, which it is foolish to pray for, when you can obtain it from yourself. There is no need to lift up your hands to heaven, nor to entreat the temple-keeper to admit us to the ear of the image, as though we could be better heard so; the god is near you, is with you, is within you.

Has that man now persuaded you that he is a good man? And yet a good man can neither so quickly come to be, nor be recognized. Do you know whom I now call a good man? One of this second rank. For that other, perhaps, like the phoenix, is born once in five hundred years. Nor is it any wonder that great things are produced at long intervals; mediocre things, and such as are born for the crowd, fortune often brings forth, but the exceptional it commends by its very rarity.

You ask how this came to me, who told me that you were planning what you had told to no one? He who knows most—rumour. "What then?" you say, "am I so great that I can stir up rumour?" There is no reason for you to measure yourself by looking to this place; look to the place in which you dwell.

Again you make yourself out a little man to me and say that Nature dealt grudgingly with you first, then fortune, when you can withdraw yourself from the common herd and rise to the highest happiness of men. If there is any other good thing in philosophy, it is this, that it does not look into the family tree. All men, if they are recalled to their first origin, come from the gods.

You complain that there is a scarcity of books there. It matters not how many you have, but how good; well-defined reading profits, varied reading delights. He who wishes to reach the place he has set out for should follow one road, not wander over many. To go thus is not to journey, but to stray.

I have received the book you promised me, and, intending to read it at my leisure, I opened it and wished only to taste it. Then it itself coaxed me to go further. How eloquent it was you may understand from this: it seemed light to me, though it was of a bulk that belonged neither to my body nor to yours, but such as at first sight might seem either Titus Livius's or Epicurus's. But it held and drew me with so great a sweetness that I read it through without any delay. The sun invited me out, hunger reminded me, the clouds threatened; yet I drank it all in.

Gladly have I learned, from those who come from you, that you live on familiar terms with your slaves. This befits your good sense, this your learning. "They are slaves." Nay, men. "They are slaves." Nay, companions of your roof. "They are slaves." Nay, humble friends. "They are slaves." Nay, fellow slaves, if you consider that fortune has just as much power over both.

To the letter you sent me on your journey, as long as the journey itself was, I shall write back later. I must withdraw apart and consider what to advise. For you too, who consult me, took thought a long while whether to consult; how much more must I do this, since longer delay is needed to untie a question than to propose one—especially since one thing is to your advantage, another to mine. Am I again speaking like an Epicurean?

He is indeed a slothful and careless man, my Lucilius, who is brought to remember a friend only when prompted by some region. Yet at times familiar places call forth the longing stored away in our mind, and do not restore an extinguished memory, but rouse one that was at rest, just as the grief of mourners, even if it has been softened by time, is renewed by a slave who was a favourite of the lost one, or by his garment, or by his house. Lo, Campania, and above all Naples and the sight of your beloved Pompeii, have made my longing for you fresh again—it is past belief; you are wholly before my eyes. I am in the very act of parting from you. I see you choking back your tears and not resisting enough the feelings that break out even amid your effort to restrain them. I seem to have lost you but a moment ago.

I received your letter many months after you had sent it. So I thought it superfluous to ask the man who brought it how you were faring. For he has a very good memory, if he remembers! And yet I hope that you now live in such a way that, wherever you are, I know what you are doing. For what else are you doing than making yourself daily better, laying aside some of your errors, understanding that those are your own faults which you suppose to be the faults of circumstances? For we ascribe certain things to places and times. But those faults, wherever we go, will follow us.

Each of us does what he can, my dear Lucilius! You there have Etna, that lofty and most famous mountain of Sicily; why Messala called it unique, or Valgius (for I have read it in both), I cannot make out, since a great many places belch fire — not only the lofty ones, as happens more often (because, of course, fire is carried up to the greatest height), but the low-lying ones as well. As for me, I make do as I can, content with Baiae — which I left the very day after I reached it; a place to be shunned, for, although it has certain natural endowments, luxury has claimed it for her own resort.

What is this, Lucilius, that drags us one way while we are striving another, and drives us toward the very place from which we long to retreat? What is it that wrestles with our mind and does not let us will anything once and for all? We are tossed about among shifting resolutions. We will nothing freely, nothing absolutely, nothing for good.

What is there that I cannot be persuaded to do, when I let myself be persuaded to go to sea? I set sail on a sluggish water. The sky, to be sure, was heavy with dirty clouds, the kind that commonly dissolve either into rain or into wind. But I thought that the few miles from your Parthenope as far as Puteoli could be slipped through, however doubtful and threatening the sky. And so, to get clear the more quickly, I headed straight out across the deep toward Nesis, meaning to cut off all the bays.

Ill health had granted me a long furlough; then it suddenly attacked me. "With what kind of attack?" you ask. You ask with perfect right; there is indeed no kind unknown to me. Yet to one disease I am, so to speak, assigned, which I do not know why I should call by a Greek name; for it can fitly enough be called "the gasping." Its onset is very brief and like a squall; within the hour or so it usually ends. For who can be drawing his last breath for long?

I have just come from a ride in my sedan, no less tired than if I had walked as far as I sat. For it is a labor to be carried even for long, and perhaps the greater because it is against Nature, who gave us feet that we might walk by ourselves, eyes that we might see by ourselves. Our soft living has condemned us to weakness, and what for a long while we refused to do, we have ceased to be able to do.

May I perish if silence is as necessary to a man set apart for study as it seems. See, a medley of noise rings round me on every side. I lodge right over a bathhouse. Now picture to yourself every kind of sound that can bring the ears to loathing: when the stronger fellows exercise and throw about their hands weighted with lead, when they either labor or pretend to labor, I hear their groans; whenever they let out the breath they have held, I hear the hissing and the harshest gasps for air. When I light on some lazy one content with the common rub-down, I hear the smack of the hand striking the shoulders, which changes its sound according as it falls flat or hollowed. But if a ball-player comes upon the scene and begins to count his throws, then it is all up with me.

When I had to make my way back from Baiae to Naples, I readily believed there was a storm, so as not to try the boat a second time; and there was so much mud along the whole road that I might seem to have gone by sea none the less. That whole day I had to endure the lot of athletes: after the wrestler's oil came the dust upon us, in the tunnel of Naples.

How great is the poverty of words for us — nay, the destitution — I never understood more than today. A thousand things came up, while we happened to be speaking of Plato, which needed names and had none; and some which, when they had once had names, had lost them through our fastidiousness. But who can endure fastidiousness in poverty?

I have taken great pleasure from your letter; allow me to use the word in its everyday sense, and do not recall it to its Stoic meaning. We hold that pleasure is a vice. So be it; yet we are accustomed to use the word to indicate a cheerful disposition of the mind.

I complain, I quarrel, I am angry. Do you even now wish for what your nurse wished for you, or your tutor, or your mother? Do you not yet understand how much evil they wished you? O how hostile to us are the prayers of our own people! And the more hostile the more happily they have turned out. I no longer wonder that all evils have followed us from earliest boyhood; we grew up amid the curses of our parents. May the gods at last hear our own voice too, raised on our behalf and asking for nothing.

Let us cease to will what we have willed. I at least am doing this: as an old man I have ceased to will the things I willed as a boy. To this one end the days go, to this the nights; this is my work, this my meditation: to set an end to old faults. I am at pains to make each day stand for a whole life. And, by Hercules, I do not snatch at it as though it were my last, but I look upon it as one that might even be the last.

They lie who wish it to seem that a throng of business stands in the way of their liberal studies; they feign their occupations, and multiply them, and busy themselves with their own selves. I am at leisure, Lucilius, I am at leisure, and wherever I am, there I am my own man. For I do not hand myself over to affairs, but lend myself, nor do I go hunting for reasons to waste time. And in whatever place I have taken my stand, there I work over my thoughts and turn over in my mind something wholesome.

I am grieved that your friend Flaccus has died, but I would not have you grieve more than is fitting. That you should not grieve at all, I shall scarcely dare to demand; and yet I know it is better. But who will attain such firmness of mind unless he is already lifted far above fortune? Even such a man this matter will pinch — but only pinch. We, however, may be pardoned for slipping into tears, provided they have not run down in excess, provided we have ourselves checked them. The eyes should be neither dry when a friend is lost, nor flooded. There should be weeping, not wailing.

You were with us yesterday. You may complain, if only yesterday. That is why I added "with us." For with me you are always. Some friends had come in, on whose account a larger smoke was made — not the kind that is wont to burst from the kitchens of the fashionable and frighten the night-watch, but a modest one, such as signifies that guests have come.

I divided yesterday with my ill health; it claimed the forenoon for itself, and yielded the afternoon to me. So first I tested my mind with reading. Then, when it had borne this, I dared to command it more — nay, to allow it more; I wrote something, and indeed more intently than usual, while I contend with a difficult subject and am unwilling to be conquered, until friends came in to use force on me and to restrain me like a sick man who has no self-control.

I have seen Claranus, my old schoolfellow, after many years. You do not expect, I think, that I should add "an old man"; but, by Hercules, his mind is green and vigorous, and he wrestles with his frail little body. For Nature dealt unfairly and lodged so great a spirit in an ill place; or perhaps she wished to show us this very thing, that a most brave and blessed genius can lie hidden under any sort of skin. Yet he overcomes all hindrances, and from contempt of himself comes to despise everything else.

To begin from things commonplace: spring has begun to open, but, now about to incline toward summer, when it ought to be warm it has only grown mild, and there is as yet no trusting it. For it often rolls back into winter. Do you wish to know how doubtful it still is? I do not yet trust myself to truly cold water; even now I break the chill of it. "This," you say, "is to endure neither hot nor cold." So it is, my dear Lucilius; my age is now content with its own coldness. Scarcely in midsummer does it thaw.

I fall in with your plan: hide yourself in retirement. But hide the retirement itself as well. That you will be doing this by the example, even if not by the precept, of the Stoics, you may know. But you will do it by the precept too; you will justify it both to yourself and to whomever you wish.

I do not want you to change your place and leap from one spot to another; first, because so frequent a removal belongs to an unstable mind. It cannot grow firm in retirement unless it ceases to look about and to wander. That you may be able to hold your mind in, first halt the flight of your body.

After a long interval I have seen your Pompeii again. I was brought back into the sight of my own youth. Whatever I had done there as a young man, I seemed to myself still able to do, and to have done a little while ago.

You keep consulting me on particular matters, forgetting that a vast sea divides us. Since a great part of counsel lies in timing, it must needs come about that on certain matters my opinion is carried to you when the contrary is already the better. For counsels are fitted to circumstances. Our affairs are borne along — nay, are whirled. Therefore counsel ought to be born on the very day; and even this is too slow; let it be born, as they say, under the hand. How it may be found, I will show.

What you ask of me was once clear to me, so well had I learned the matter through and through. But I have not retested my memory for a long while, and so it does not easily follow me. What happens to books that have stuck together from disuse, this I feel has happened to me; my mind must be unfolded, and whatever has been laid up in it must be shaken out from time to time, that it may be ready as often as need shall demand. Let us therefore put this off for the present; for it requires much labor, much care. As soon as I hope for a longer stay in the same place, then I shall take it in hand.

They seem to me to err who think that those faithfully devoted to philosophy are stubborn and refractory, despisers of magistrates or kings or of those by whom public affairs are administered. For, on the contrary, none are more grateful toward them; and not without reason. For to none do they owe more than to those by whose grace they may enjoy untroubled leisure.

Your letter delighted me and roused me from my languor; it also called forth my memory, which is now sluggish and slow with me. Why should you not, my dear Lucilius, think this the greatest instrument of the happy life — the conviction that there is one good, that which is honorable? For he who judges other things to be goods comes into the power of fortune, becomes subject to another's will; but he who has circumscribed every good within the honorable is happy within himself.

You complain that letters are sent to you by me with too little care. For who speaks with care, unless he wishes to speak affectedly? Such as my talk would be if we were sitting or walking together — unlabored and easy — such I wish my letters to be, which have nothing fetched in or feigned.

You threaten me with hostility if I keep you in the dark about any of my daily doings. See, then, how openly I live with you: I shall confide even this. I am attending the lectures of a philosopher; this is now the fifth day that I have been going to his school and listening to him hold forth from the eighth hour. "A fine age to begin!" you say. Fine indeed. And what is more foolish than to refuse to learn simply because you have not learned for a long time?

Today, all of a sudden, the Alexandrian ships came into view, the ones usually sent ahead to announce the coming of the fleet behind them; they are called the mail-boats. Campania is glad to see them; the whole crowd stands out on the piers of Puteoli and picks out the Alexandrian vessels from the very style of their sails, even among a great throng of ships. For they alone are allowed to spread the topsail, which in the open sea all ships carry.

That you are plagued by frequent catarrhs and the little fevers that follow long-standing and habitual catarrhs distresses me the more because I have had experience of this kind of ill health, which at first I made light of; my youth could still bear injuries and carry itself stubbornly against disease. Then I gave way and was brought to such a pass that I dripped away myself, reduced to the extreme of leanness.

I am waiting for your letters, in which you may tell me what new sights your tour around the whole of Sicily has shown you, and above all some surer information about Charybdis itself. For that Scylla is a rock, and indeed not one to be feared by sailors, I know very well; but whether Charybdis answers to the stories told of it I should like you to write to me, and, if you have observed it, since the thing is worth the watching, to inform me whether it is whipped up by one wind only, or whether every storm equally churns up that sea, and whether it is true that whatever is caught in that whirlpool's eddy is carried under the water for many miles and only thrown up again near the shore of Tauromenium.

Today I am free, and not only by my own good leave but by that of the show, which has called away all the troublesome to a boxing-match. No one will burst in, no one will hinder my thinking, which, on the strength of this very confidence, advances the more boldly. The door has not creaked from time to time, the curtain will not be raised; I may go safely, which is the more necessary for one who walks by his own path and follows his own way. Am I not, then, following those before me? Yes; but I allow myself to find something too, to change something, to throw something out. I am not their slave, though I am their approver.

You complain that you have fallen in with an ungrateful man. If this is the first time, give thanks either to your fortune or to your care. But in this matter care can do nothing except make you grudging. For if you wish to avoid this danger, you will give no benefits; and so, that they may not be lost upon another, they will be lost upon you. Better that there be no return than that none be given. Even after a bad harvest one must sow; often the abundance of a single year restores all that had been lost through the unbroken barrenness of an unlucky soil.

I have now ceased to be anxious about you. "Which of the gods," you ask, "have you taken as your surety?" That one, of course, who deceives no one, a mind that loves the right and the good. The better part of you is in safety. Fortune can do you an injury; what concerns the matter more, I do not fear that you will do one to yourself. Go where you have begun to go, and settle yourself into that mode of life calmly, not softly.

You bid me set out for you my single days, and indeed in their entirety; you judge well of me, if you think there is nothing in them which I would hide. So at any rate we ought to live, as though we lived in the sight of others; so we ought to think, as though someone could look into our inmost breast, and indeed someone can. For what does it profit that something is kept secret from a man? Nothing is closed to God. He is present at our minds and enters into the midst of our thoughts, into the midst, I say, as one who at some time departs.

These travels of mine, which shake my sluggishness out of me, I judge to be good both for my health and for my studies. Why they help my health you see: since my love of letters makes me lazy and careless of my body, I take exercise by another's labour. Why they should be good for studies I will show you: I have not withdrawn from my reading. Reading, in my opinion, is necessary, first that I may not be content with myself alone, then that, when I have learned what others have inquired into, I may both pass judgment on what has been discovered and think out what is still to be discovered. Reading nourishes the mind and refreshes it when it is wearied with study, though not without study itself.

I had spared you, and had passed over whatever knotty matter still remained, content to give you, as it were, a taste of the things said by our school, to prove that virtue alone is effective enough to fill out the happy life. You bid me embrace whatever there is of questions, whether ours or those devised to refute us. If I should wish to do this, it will be not a letter but a book. This I declare again and again, that I take no delight in this kind of argument. I am ashamed to go down into the line of battle, undertaken on behalf of gods and men, armed with a cobbler's awl.

I write this to you as I lie in the very villa of Scipio Africanus, having paid my respects to his shade and to the altar which I suspect is the tomb of so great a man. As for his soul, I persuade myself that it has returned to heaven, from which it came, not because he led great armies, for these the frenzied Cambyses too had, who used his frenzy with success, but on account of his remarkable moderation and devotion, which I judge more admirable in him when he left his country than when he defended it; for either Scipio had to be at Rome, or Rome in freedom.

I made shipwreck before I went aboard the ship. How it happened I do not add, lest you think this too is to be set among the Stoic paradoxes, none of which, I will prove to you when you wish, nay even when you do not wish, is false or so marvellous as at first sight it appears. Meanwhile this journey taught me how many superfluous things we have, and how easily, by a judgment of our own, we can lay down things which, if at any time necessity has taken them away, we do not feel their loss.

You desire to know what I think about the liberal studies. I admire none of them, I count none among the goods, which has money for its end. They are hireling trades, useful so far as they prepare the mind, not detain it. For we must dwell on these things only so long as the mind can do nothing greater; they are our apprenticeship, not our work.

You desire a useful thing, and one necessary for a man hastening toward wisdom, that philosophy be divided and its vast body distributed into its members. For we more easily come to know the whole through its parts. Would that philosophy itself, like the whole face of the universe, came into our view all at once! It would furnish us a sight very like that of the world. Surely it would then hold all mortals in admiration of itself, and we should lay aside those things which now, ignorant of the great, we think great.

Who can doubt, my Lucilius, that it is the gift of the immortal gods that we live, but of philosophy that we live well? And so it would be held for certain that we owe so much more to her than to the gods, by how much a good life is a greater benefit than life, were it not that the gods themselves bestowed philosophy. The knowledge of it they have given to none, but the faculty of attaining it to all.

Our friend Liberalis is now downcast at the news of the fire by which the colony of Lyons was burned up. This disaster might move anyone, much more a man most loving toward his native city. And it is this that has made him seek the firmness of his own mind, which, no doubt, he had trained for those things which he thought could be feared. But that this evil, so unlooked-for and almost unheard-of, should have caught him without fear, I do not wonder, since it was without precedent. For fire has plagued many cities, but destroyed none. For even where the buildings have been kindled by an enemy's hand, the fire dies out in many places, and, though often revived, rarely devours the whole, so that scarcely anything is so destroyed that the wreckage stands as a memorial. An earthquake has hardly overthrown so many and such great buildings; nowhere has a fire blazed so fiercely as to leave nothing for the next; in one night so beautiful a city has fallen that you might say it had never stood.

I think it will be agreed between you and me that external things are acquired for the body, the body is tended in honour of the mind, and that in the mind there are serving parts, through which we move and are nourished, given to us for the sake of the ruling part itself. In this ruling part there is something irrational, and something rational. The former serves the latter; the latter is the one thing that is not referred to another, but refers all things to itself.

In the letter in which you lamented the death of the philosopher Metronax, as though he both could and ought to have lived longer, I missed that fairness of yours which abounds in you toward every person and in every affair, but is lacking in one matter, the one in which it is lacking to all. I have found many men fair toward men, none toward the gods. We chide fate daily: "Why was that man snatched away in mid-course? Why is that other not snatched away? Why does he prolong an old age burdensome both to himself and to others?"

That part of philosophy which gives to each person his own precepts, and does not shape man in the general, but counsels the husband how to bear himself toward his wife, the father how to rear his children, the master how to govern his slaves, some have accepted alone, leaving the rest as though wandering outside our advantage, as if anyone could give counsel about a part who had not first embraced the sum of the whole of life.

You ask me to bring forward at once, and write to you, what I had said should be put off to its own day, whether this part of philosophy which the Greeks call paraenetic, and we the preceptive, is enough to bring wisdom to its completion. I know that you will take it in good part if I refuse. But I shall the more readily promise it, and shall not let the proverb perish: 'Do not ask afterward for what you would not wish to obtain.'

And yet are you indignant at something, or complaining, and do you not understand that there is nothing of evil in those things except this one thing, that you are indignant and complaining? If you ask me, I think nothing wretched for a man unless there is something in the nature of things which he thinks wretched. I shall not endure myself on the day when I shall not be able to endure something. I am in ill health; it is a part of fate. My household has fallen sick, my loans have struck a snag, my house has cracked, losses, wounds, toils, fears have run upon me; it is wont to happen. This is too little; it ought to have happened.

You are mistaken, my Lucilius, if you think that luxury and the neglect of good morals and the other things which each man has charged against his own times are a vice of our age; these belong to men, not to times. No age has been free of fault. And if you begin to weigh the licence of any one age, it is shameful to say it, never was sin committed more openly than in the presence of Cato.

Never believe anyone happy who hangs upon his good fortune. He leans on fragile things who is glad at what came from outside; the joy will go out which came in. But that joy which has sprung from oneself is faithful and firm, and grows, and accompanies us to the very end; the rest, whose admiration is among the crowd, are goods for the day. 'What then? Cannot they be of use and of pleasure?' Who denies it? But only in this way, if they depend on us, not we on them.

The letter which I wrote to Marullus, when he had lost his little son and was said to be bearing it weakly, I have sent to you; in it I did not follow the usual custom, nor did I think that he ought to be handled gently, since he was more worthy of rebuke than of consolation. For to one stricken and bearing ill a great wound, one must yield for a little while; let him sate himself, or at least pour out the first onset; but those who have taken upon themselves to mourn should be chastised at once, and learn that there are certain follies even in tears.

Show me anyone who sets some price upon his time, who reckons the worth of a day, who understands that he is dying daily. For in this we are deceived, that we look ahead to death; much of it has already gone by. Whatever span of life lies behind us, death holds it. So do, my Lucilius, what you write that you are doing: lay hold of every hour. Thus it will come about that you hang less upon tomorrow, if you set your hand upon today. While it is being put off, life races by.

But take care that this reading of many authors and of books of every kind does not carry with it something wandering and unsteady. You must dwell upon and feed yourself upon certain master minds, if you would draw out anything that will lodge faithfully in the mind. He who is everywhere is nowhere. To those who spend their life in travel it happens that they have many lodgings but no friendships. The same thing must befall those who attach themselves intimately to no one's genius, but pass over everything in haste and at a run.

But if you consider anyone a friend in whom you do not trust as much as in yourself, you are gravely mistaken, and you do not sufficiently know the force of true friendship. With a friend, indeed, deliberate about everything, but first about the friend himself. After friendship begins, you must trust; before friendship, you must judge. Those men confound their duties in the wrong order who, against the precepts of Theophrastus, judge after they have come to love, and do not love after they have judged. Consider long whether anyone is to be received into your friendship. When it has pleased you that it should be, admit him with your whole heart; speak as boldly with him as with yourself.

You surely keep in memory how great a joy you felt when, laying aside the bordered toga of boyhood, you put on the toga of manhood and were escorted into the forum; expect a greater joy when you have laid aside the boyish mind and philosophy has enrolled you among men. For as yet it is not boyhood, but, what is more serious, childishness that remains; and this is the worse, that we have the authority of old men together with the faults of boys—and not of boys only, but of infants. They fear trifling things, infants fear false things, while we fear both.

Avoid a rough exterior, an unshorn head, a too-neglected beard, a professed hatred of silver, a bed laid on the bare ground, and whatever else a perverse ambition pursues by the wrong road. The very name of philosophy is hateful enough, even if it is handled with moderation; what if we begin to set ourselves apart from the usage of mankind? Let everything within be unlike the crowd, but let our outward face match the people's.

And so I should wish to share with you this so sudden change in myself; then I should begin to have a surer confidence in our friendship—that true friendship which neither hope nor fear nor concern for its own advantage tears apart, that friendship with which men die, for which they die.

The company of many is harmful: there is no one who does not either recommend to us some vice, or stamp it upon us, or smear it on us while we are unaware. And surely the larger the throng we mingle with, the greater the danger. But nothing is so ruinous to good morals as to lounge at some show. For then, through pleasure, the vices steal in more easily.

I have withdrawn not only from men, but from affairs, and chiefly from my own affairs; I am doing the business of posterity. For them I write down some things that may be of use. Wholesome admonitions, like the prescriptions of useful medicines, I commit to writing, having found them effective upon my own sores, which, even if they are not wholly healed, have at least ceased to spread.

We are bound to fall into ambiguity if we wish to render the Greek apatheia hastily by a single word and to say "impassibility." For the opposite of what we mean may be understood. We mean to describe the man who rejects all sense of evil; but he will be taken to mean the man who can endure no evil. See, then, whether it is not better to speak of an "invulnerable mind," or a "mind placed beyond all suffering."

We are accustomed to keep watch over the man who is in mourning or in fear, lest he make a bad use of his solitude. There is no one among the unwise who ought to be left to himself; then it is that they hatch evil plans, then they contrive future dangers either for others or for themselves, then they marshal their wicked desires, then the mind lays bare whatever it was concealing through fear or shame, then it whets its boldness, inflames its lust, goads its anger. In short, the one advantage that solitude has—to confide in no one, to fear no informer—is lost upon the fool; he betrays himself. See, then, what I hope for you—nay, what I pledge to myself, for hope is the name of an uncertain good: I find no one with whom I would rather have you be than with yourself.

He plainly confesses and prefers this, that he is not over-finished. But, as you say, the matter itself, not the mind, drew forth those words. You will find nothing slack, nothing low; the words are choice, not hunted, nor, after the fashion of this age, set against their own nature and turned inside out; yet splendid, though taken from common speech. You will find noble sentiments, expressed nobly, though not pointed into epigrams. We shall see in this man what is wanting, what is uneven, what stands out beyond the polish of our age; but when you have surveyed the whole, you will find nothing empty.

Money too lingers longest about poverty, while it is still struggling free of it and clings there. By now Senecio was reaching toward riches, to which two most effective qualities were leading him, the knowledge both of getting and of keeping, either one of which by itself could have made him wealthy.

It was a delight to inquire about the eternity of souls, nay, by Hercules, to believe in it. For I was lending a ready ear to the opinions of great men, who promised, rather than proved, a thing most welcome. I was giving myself up to so great a hope. Already I was growing weary of myself, already I despised the remnants of a broken span of life, as one about to pass into that boundless stretch of time and into possession of all the ages; when suddenly I was awakened by the receipt of your letter, and lost so fair a dream. But I shall resume it once I have dismissed you, and shall buy it back.

And the storm threatens before it rises, buildings crack before they fall, smoke gives warning of fire; but the ruin that comes from man is sudden, and is concealed the more carefully the nearer it draws. You are mistaken if you trust the faces of those you meet; they have the looks of men, the hearts of beasts, save that with beasts only the first onset is deadly; those they have passed by, they do not seek out. For nothing but necessity ever goads beasts to do harm; either by hunger or by fear they are driven to the fight; but to man it is a pleasure to destroy man.

This I said to my Paulina, who bids me take care of my health. For since I know that her breath of life is bound up in mine, I begin, in order to look after her, to look after myself. And although old age has made me braver against many things, I am losing this benefit of my years, for it comes into my mind that within this old man there is also a youth, who is spared. And so, since I cannot prevail upon her to love me more bravely, she prevails upon me to love myself more carefully.

Of all these, contempt is so much the slightest that many have taken refuge in it as a remedy. Whomever a man despises, he wrongs no doubt, but he passes him by; no one harms a man he despises persistently, no one harms him carefully. Even in the battle-line the man who lies down is passed over; the fight is with the man who stands.

For you know that I wish to embrace moral philosophy and to unfold all the questions belonging to it. And so I doubted whether to put you off, until its proper place came round for this matter, or to give you a ruling out of turn; it seemed more humane not to keep waiting one who came from so far.

It moulds and shapes the mind, orders life, governs our actions, points out what is to be done and what left undone, sits at the helm and steers the course of those who waver amid perilous straits. Without it no one can live undaunted, no one secure. Countless things happen every hour that demand counsel, which must be sought from her.

It remains for me to divide the rational part of philosophy. All speech is either continuous or broken between one who answers and one who questions. I have you as the pattern of the picture, from which our mind takes a certain form to impose upon its work. So that face which teaches and instructs me, from which the imitation is sought, is the Idea. Such patterns, then, the nature of things has in infinite number — of men, fish, trees — according to which whatever must be made by her is fashioned.
