They will have some price, but no dignity; they will stand apart by great intervals among themselves; some will be smaller, some greater.

As in bodies the signs of a settling languor run ahead — for there is a certain nerveless sluggishness and a weariness without any toil, and yawning, and a shudder running through the limbs — so the weak mind is shaken long before it is overwhelmed by evils. It anticipates them and falls before its time. But what is more mad than to be tortured by things future and not to reserve oneself for the torment, but to summon miseries to oneself and bring them near?

If he looks with steady eyes upon flashing swords, and knows that it makes no difference to him whether his breath goes out through his mouth or through his slit throat, call him happy; if, when the tortures of the body are threatened against him, both those that come by chance and those that come by the wrong of a stronger man, when chains and exile and the empty terrors of human minds are spoken of, he hears them unmoved and says: "No shape of toils, O maiden, rises before me new or unforeseen; I have foretasted all and gone through them with myself in my mind. You threaten me with these things today; I have always threatened myself with them, and have prepared myself, a man, for what is human."

I judge that the answer must be made otherwise: that neither is the helmsman's art made worse by any storm, nor the very practice of the art. The helmsman has promised you not good fortune, but useful service and the knowledge of steering a ship. This appears the more, the more some chance force has resisted him. He who could say, "Neptune, never shall you sink this ship except upright," has done justice to his art; the storm does not hinder the helmsman's work, but his success.

'In that way,' he says, 'riches are even an evil, not merely not a good.' They would be an evil, they would themselves do harm, if, as I said, they had an efficient cause; as it is, they have an antecedent one, and one not merely inciting minds, but attracting them. For they pour over us an appearance of good, like to the true and credible to most men.

Wisdom is a great and spacious thing. It needs empty room. One must learn about things divine and human, about the past and the future, about things perishable and eternal, about time. Concerning this one thing alone, see how many questions are asked: first, whether it is anything in itself; then, whether anything is before time and without time; whether it began with the world, or, because there was something even before the world, time too existed.

It has escaped you, moreover, that the same Democritus discovered how ivory might be softened, how a baked pebble might be turned into emerald, by which method even today stones that are found suitable are baked into colour. Granting that a wise man found these things out, yet he did not find them as a wise man; for he does many things which we see done as skilfully, or even more skilfully, by the most unskilled.

When it has borne itself up to this height, the body too it tends not from love but from care, as a needful thing, and is unwilling to be subject to that which it rules. For no one is free who is a slave to the body, who is even sold for it. For, that I may pass over the other masters whom excessive care of it finds, its sway is fickle, dainty.

'Expel,' he says, 'false opinions about goods and evils, and put true ones in their place, and admonition will have nothing to do.' The mind is no doubt set in order by this method, but not by this alone. For although it is gathered by arguments which things are goods and evils, nevertheless precepts have their own parts. Both prudence and justice consist of duties; duties are arranged by precepts.

Now there is need of swift hands, now of masterly art. Pleasure is sought from everything. No vice stays within itself; luxury rushes headlong into avarice. Forgetfulness of the honourable has come upon us. Nothing is base whose price pleases. Man, a thing sacred to man, is now slain for sport and jest, and one whom it was a crime to train for the giving and receiving of wounds is now brought forth naked and unarmed, and the death of a man is spectacle enough.

We can, then, have as much spirit against these things, if only we are willing to draw our neck from the yoke. But above all pleasures must be rejected; they unman and unstring us, and demand much, and much must be demanded of fortune. Next, riches must be scorned: they are the bonds of slaveries. Let gold and silver, and whatever else weighs down prosperous houses, be left behind; liberty cannot be had for nothing. If you value this highly, all else must be valued at little. Farewell.

Then he thinks himself fortunate that he has found whence it seemed good to Virgil to say: "over whom the huge gate of heaven thunders." Ennius, he says, filched this from Homer, and Virgil from Ennius. For there is in Cicero, in these very books On the Commonwealth, this epigram of Ennius: "If it is right for anyone to ascend to the regions of the heavenly ones, for me alone the great gate of heaven lies open."

But if the body is useless for its services, why should it not be fitting to lead forth the laboring soul? And perhaps it must be done a little before one ought, lest, when one ought to do it, one be unable. And since there is greater danger in living badly than in dying quickly, he is a fool who does not buy off the hazard of a great matter for the small price of a little time. Long old age has carried few to death without injury; to many an inactive life has lain useless, with no enjoyment of itself; how much crueler, then, do you judge it to have lost something out of life than to have lost the right of ending it?

Just as all good men are equal in so far as they are good. But they have differences of age: one is older, another younger; differences of body: one is handsome, another deformed; differences of fortune: this one is rich, that one poor; this one in favor, powerful, known to cities and peoples, that one unknown to most and obscure. But through that by which they are good, they are equal.

And among those who pursue wisdom themselves we must confess there are great distinctions. One has now advanced so far that he dares to lift his eyes against fortune, but not steadfastly, for they fall, dazzled by too great a splendor; another so far that he can match his countenance with hers — unless he has already arrived at the summit and is full of confidence.

Which it is best to put off, if one cannot dispel them. Do you wish to know that no one ought to be tortured by the future? Whoever has heard that he must suffer punishments after his fiftieth year is not perturbed unless he has leaped over the intervening space and flung himself into that anxiety to come an age later; in the same way it comes about that things old and obliterated sadden minds gladly sick and grasping at causes of grief. Both things that have passed and things that are to come are absent; we feel neither. But there is no pain except from what you feel. Farewell.

The blow of an evil foreseen falls softly. But to fools, and to those who trust in fortune, every shape of things seems new and unlooked for; and among the inexperienced a large part of an evil lies in its novelty. That you may know this, men endure more bravely, once they have grown used to them, the things they had thought harsh.

"What then?" he says, "does not that thing harm the helmsman which forbids him to make harbour, which renders his efforts vain, which either carries him back or holds him fast and dismasts him?" It harms him not as a helmsman, but as a voyager; otherwise he is not a helmsman. So far is it from hindering the helmsman's art that it displays it; for, as the saying is, "in calm weather anyone is a helmsman." These things are adverse to the ship, not to the steersman, in so far as he is a steersman.

Virtue too has an antecedent cause that draws on envy; for many envy wisdom on account of justice. But it neither has this cause from itself nor a probable one. For, on the contrary, that appearance which virtue casts upon the minds of men is more probable, an appearance that calls them to love and admiration.

There are countless questions about the soul alone: whence it is, what it is, when it begins to be, how long it is; whether it passes from one place to another and changes its dwelling, transferred into the shapes of other animals one after another, or serves only once and then, set free, wanders through the universe; whether it is body or not; what it will do when it ceases to act through us; how it will use its freedom when it has fled this prison; whether it forgets things past and then begins to know itself, when, parted from the body, it has withdrawn on high.

Do you ask what the wise man has investigated, what he has dragged into the light? First, the truth and nature, which he followed, not as the other animals, with eyes slow toward things divine. Then the law of life, which he directed to the whole, and he taught not only to know but to follow the gods, and to receive what befalls no otherwise than as things commanded. He forbade us to obey false opinions, and weighed by a true valuation how much each thing was worth. He condemned pleasures mingled with repentance, and praised goods that would always please, and made it plain that the happiest man is he who has no need of happiness, the most powerful he who has himself in his power.

From this body the mind goes forth now with an even temper, now leaps out, and does not then inquire what the end of the abandoned body is to be. But as we take no heed of shavings from the beard and hair, so that divine mind, about to go out of the man, considers it indifferent whither its lodging shall be borne, whether fire burns it up, or stone shuts it in, or earth presses it down, or wild beasts tear it. "It is no more its concern than the afterbirth is the concern of a newborn child." Whether thrown out, the body lies a prey to the birds, or is consumed, "given as spoil to the dogs of the sea," what is that to one who is nothing?

Besides, the very judgment about goods and evils is confirmed by the doing of duty, and to this admonition leads. For both follow each other: precept cannot exist unless the judgment about goods and evils has gone before, and this very judgment is made fuller by precept.

In this perversity of morals, then, something more vehement than usual is needed, which may scatter the inveterate evils; we must work with decrees, that the received persuasion of false things may be torn out by the roots. If to these we join precepts, consolations, exhortations, they will be able to avail; by themselves they are ineffective.

But, that I myself, while I do something else, may not slip into being a philologist or a grammarian, I give this warning: that the hearing and reading of philosophers should be turned to the purpose of the happy life, not that we may hunt for ancient or coined words, or improper metaphors and figures of speech, but for precepts that will profit and for magnificent and spirited utterances, which may soon be transferred into action. Let us so learn these things that what have been words may become works.

Do not hear me unwillingly, as though this judgment already concerned you, but weigh what I say: I will not abandon old age, if it keeps me whole for myself — whole, that is, on that better side; but if it begins to shake my mind, to tear away its parts, if it leaves me not life but mere breath, I will leap forth from the rotten and tottering building.

The senses do not judge of goods and evils; what is useful, what useless, they do not know. They cannot pass sentence unless they are brought into the presence of the thing. They are neither provident of the future nor mindful of the past; what is consequent, they do not know. But from this is woven the order and seat of things and the unity of a life that is to proceed along the straight path. Reason, then, is the arbiter of goods and evils; it holds outward and external things as worthless, and judges those things which are neither good nor evil to be the smallest and slightest accessories. For to it every good is in the mind.

Imperfect things must needs totter, and now advance, now slip back or sink down. And they will slip back unless they persevere in going and striving; if they relax anything from their zeal and faithful intentness, they must go backward. No one finds his progress where he left it. Let us therefore press on and persevere.

Therefore the wise man grows accustomed to coming evils, and what others make light by long endurance, he makes light by long forethought. Sometimes we hear the voices of the inexperienced saying, "I knew it was in store for me"; the wise man knows that all things are in store for him. Whatever has happened, he says: "I knew it." Farewell.

The helmsman has two characters: one common to him with all who have gone aboard the same ship: he too is a passenger; the other peculiar to him: he is the helmsman. The storm harms him as a passenger, not as a helmsman.

Posidonius says one must put the question thus: 'Things which give the mind neither greatness nor confidence nor security are not goods. But riches and good health and the like do none of these things; therefore they are not goods.' This question he presses even more strongly now in this way: 'Things which give the mind neither greatness nor confidence nor security, but on the contrary create insolence, swelling, arrogance, are evils. But by the gifts of chance we are driven into these things; therefore they are not goods.'

Whatever part of things human and divine you grasp, you will be wearied by a vast abundance of things to be inquired into and learned. That these things, so many, so great, may have a free lodging, the superfluous must be cleared from the mind. Virtue will not give itself into these straits; a great thing requires a roomy space. Let all things be expelled, let the whole breast be free for it.

I speak not of that philosophy which set the citizen outside his country, the gods outside the world, which gave virtue over to pleasure, but of that which counts nothing good but the honourable, which can be bribed neither by men nor by fortune, whose price is that it cannot be bought. This philosophy I do not believe to have existed in that rude age, when as yet there was no art at all, and useful things were learned by practice itself.

But even then, while he is among men, he fears none of the threats against his body, nor those who would foully mangle the corpse for the sake of insult. "I ask no one for the last office, I commend to no one my remains. The nature of things has provided that no one should lie unburied; whomever cruelty has cast out, the day will cover." One spoke eloquently who said: "I care not for a tomb. Nature buries the abandoned." You would think a man tight-girt had said this. For he had a talent both great and manly, had he not loosened its girdle in prosperity. Farewell.

'Precepts,' he says, 'are infinite.' It is false. For about the greatest and most necessary matters they are not infinite. They have slight differences, which times, places, persons demand, but for these too general precepts are given.

If we wish to hold men bound and to tear them from the evils by which they are now held, let them learn what is evil, what is good. Let them know that all things except virtue change their name, and become now evils, now goods. As the first bond of military service is religion and love of the standards and the wickedness of desertion, and then afterward the rest are easily exacted and commanded of those who have been bound by the oath, so in those whom you would lead to the happy life, the first foundations must be laid and virtue instilled. Let them be held by a kind of superstition for it; let them love it; let them wish to live with it, refuse to live without it.

But I judge that no men deserve worse of all mortals than those who have learned philosophy as though it were some saleable craft, who live otherwise than they teach men ought to live. For they carry themselves about as examples of a useless discipline, liable to every vice which they pursue with words.

I will not flee a disease by death, provided it is curable and does not stand in the way of the mind. I will not lay hands on myself because of pain; to die thus is to be conquered. Yet if I know that I must suffer it forever, I will go out — not because of the pain itself, but because it will be a hindrance to me in all that for which one lives. Weak and cowardly is the man who dies because of pain; foolish, the man who lives for the sake of pain.

But it esteems certain goods as primary, to which it comes of set purpose, such as victory, good children, the safety of one's country. Certain it esteems secondary, which do not appear except in adversity, such as to bear with even mind a grave illness, or exile. Certain are intermediate, which are no more according to Nature than against Nature, such as to walk prudently, to sit composedly. For it is no less according to Nature to sit than to stand or to walk.

More remains than we have routed, but a great part of progress is the will to make progress. Of this thing I am conscious to myself; I will, and I will with my whole mind. You too I see to be roused and hastening with great impulse toward the fairest things. Let us hasten; only so will life be a benefit. Otherwise it is a delay, and indeed a shameful one for those who dwell among foul things. Let us see to it that all our time be our own. But it will not be, unless we first begin to be our own.

Then the helmsman's art is another's good: it concerns those whom he carries, as the physician's concerns those whom he cures. But the wise man's good is a common good: it belongs both to those among whom he lives and to himself. Therefore the helmsman may perhaps be harmed, who has promised his service to others and is hindered from rendering it; but the wise man is not harmed by poverty, not by pain, not by the other storms of life.

'By this reasoning,' he says, 'they will not even be advantageous.' The condition of advantageous things is one thing, of goods another; the advantageous is that which has more use than trouble. The good ought to be sincere and in every part harmless. That is not good which is more profitable, but that which is only profitable.

'But the knowledge of many arts delights one.' Therefore let us retain only as much of them as is necessary. Or do you think the man worthy of blame who gets together superfluous things for use and spreads out in his house a parade of costly objects, but do not think that man so who is busied with the superfluous furniture of letters? To wish to know more than is enough is a kind of intemperance.

There followed the fortunate age, before, the gods being yet propitious, the gifts of nature lay open to be used in common, before avarice and luxury sundered mortals from one another and taught them to break out into plunder instead of fellowship. Those men were not wise, though they did things which the wise do.

'No one,' he says, 'cures madness by precepts; therefore not wickedness either.' It is unlike. For if you take away madness, health returns; but false opinions about goods and evils are not removed when wickedness has been removed; one must learn what to do.

'What then? Have not some, without subtle instruction, turned out upright and attained great progress, while they obeyed bare precepts only?' I confess it; but they had a happy disposition, and snatched at saving things in passing. For as the immortal gods learned no virtue, being born with all of it, and it is a part of their nature to be good, so certain men, having been allotted an excellent disposition, come to the things which are usually handed over without long teaching, and have embraced honourable things as soon as they heard them; whence those temperaments so greedy of virtue, or fruitful of themselves. But those dull and sluggish minds, or beset by bad custom, must have their mental rust rubbed off again and again.

No such teacher can profit me any more than a helmsman who is seasick in a storm. The helm must be held while the wave snatches it, one must struggle with the very sea, the sails must be wrenched from the wind; what help to me can be a steersman of the ship who is dumbstruck and vomiting? How much greater a storm do you think life is tossed by than any vessel? One must not talk, but steer.

But I am running on too long. There is besides matter enough to spin out the day. And how shall the man be able to set an end to his life who cannot set an end to a letter? Farewell, then — which you will read more gladly than mere talk of death. Farewell.

Those two higher goods are diverse. For the first are according to Nature: to rejoice in the devotion of children, in the safety of one's country. The second are against Nature: bravely to withstand torments and to endure thirst while disease burns the vitals.

When will it fall to us to despise both kinds of fortune, when will it fall to us, all our passions crushed and brought under our own control, to send forth this cry: "I have conquered"? Whom have I conquered, you ask? Not the Persians, nor the far reaches of the Medes, nor whatever warlike thing lies beyond the Dahae, but greed, but ambition, but the fear of death, which has conquered the conquerors of nations. Farewell.

For not all his works are hindered, but only those that concern others; he himself is always in action, and then greatest when fortune has opposed itself to him. For then he does the very business of wisdom, which we said was both another's good and his own.

Besides, the advantageous belongs to animals too, and to imperfect men, and to fools. And so there can be a disadvantage mixed with it, but it is called advantageous, valued by its greater part; the good belongs to the wise man alone; it ought to be inviolate.

And what of this, that this pursuit of the liberal arts makes men troublesome, wordy, ill-timed, pleased with themselves, and for this reason not learning the necessary things, that they have learned the superfluous? The grammarian Didymus wrote four thousand books. I should pity him, had he merely read so many superfluous ones. In these books it is inquired what was Homer's country, in these who was the true mother of Aeneas, in these whether Anacreon lived more lustfully or more drunkenly, in these whether Sappho was a public woman, and other things which, if you knew them, you would have to unlearn. Go now and deny that life is long.

No one would more admire any other state of the human race, nor, if a god should permit him to fashion earthly things and give nations their manners, would he approve any other than that which is recorded to have been among those peoples among whom "no tillers subdued the fields, nor was it lawful even to mark off or divide the plain with a boundary; they sought in common, and the earth herself bore all things more freely, none demanding."

'Laws,' he says, 'do not bring it about that we do what we ought, and what else are they than precepts mixed with threats?' First of all, they do not persuade for this reason, that they threaten; but precepts do not compel, but entreat. Then laws deter from crime, precepts exhort to duty. Add to this that the laws too profit toward good morals, especially if they not only command but teach. In this matter I dissent from Posidonius, who says: 'I disapprove that prologues were added to the laws of Plato. A law ought to be brief, that it may the more easily be understood by the unskilled. Let it be a voice sent down from heaven; let it command, not dispute. Nothing seems to me colder, nothing more silly, than a law with a preface. Warn me, tell me what you wish me to do; I do not learn, I obey.' But laws of this kind profit; therefore you will see states with bad laws have bad morals.

But, just as instruction more quickly raises to the summit those who are inclined to good, so it will help these weaker ones too and draw them out of bad opinions, whoever has handed over to them the tenets of philosophy; and how necessary these are you may understand from this, that there are things which sit within us, yet do not make us ready for action. 'You ought to do this for a father, this for children, this for friends, this for guests'; while a man tries, avarice will hold him back. He knows that he must fight for his country, but fear will dissuade him; he knows that he must sweat for his friends to the very last sweat, but pleasure will forbid.

Everything they say, everything they fling about with the crowd listening, is borrowed: Plato said those things, Zeno said them, Chrysippus and Posidonius and a vast army of our school, so many and such men. How they can prove these things to be their own, I will show: let them do what they have said.

What then? Is anything against Nature a good? By no means; but that is sometimes against Nature in which that good arises. For to be wounded and to waste away under applied fire and to be stricken with ill health is against Nature; but to keep the mind untiring amid these things is according to Nature.

Besides, not even then is he forbidden to benefit others, when some necessities press upon him. Because of poverty he is forbidden to teach how the commonwealth must be managed, but he teaches this, how poverty must be managed. Through his whole life his work extends. Thus no fortune, no circumstance shuts out the activities of the wise man. For he does the very thing by which he is forbidden to do the others. He is fitted for both kinds of chance: he is the ruler of goods, the conqueror of evils.

Be of good cheer; one knot remains for you, but a Herculean one: 'Good does not come from evils. But from many instances of poverty riches come; therefore riches are not a good.' This question our school do not acknowledge; the Peripatetics both invent it and solve it. But Posidonius says that this sophism, bandied about through all the schools of the dialecticians, was thus refuted by Antipater:

But when you come to our own school too, I will show you many things that should be given to the axe. At a great expense of time, at great trouble to others' ears, this praise is bought: 'O man of letters!' Let us be content with this more rustic title: 'O good man!'

What kind of men was happier than that race? They enjoyed nature's bounty in common; she sufficed, as a parent, for the protection of all. This was the secure possession of the public wealth. Why should I not call that the richest race of mortals, in which you could find no poor man? Into things so excellently placed avarice broke in, and while it longed to set something apart and turn it to its own, it made all things another's and reduced itself from the boundless into a narrow compass. Avarice brought in poverty, and, by coveting much, lost all.
'But they do not profit with all.'

It will do no good, therefore, to give precepts, unless you have first removed the things that will stand against the precepts, no more than it will do good to have set arms in view and brought them near, unless the hands are made ready to use them. That the mind may be able to go to the precepts which we give, it must be set free.

Since I have now said what I wished to convey to you, I will now satisfy your desire, and will transfer entire into another letter the matter you had demanded, lest you come weary to a thorny subject, one to be heard with ears erect and curious. Farewell.

And, to express briefly what I mean, the material of a good is sometimes against Nature, the good never, since no good is without reason, and reason follows Nature. What, then, is reason? An imitation of Nature. What is the highest good of man? To conduct himself according to the will of Nature.

So, I say, he has trained himself to display virtue as much in prosperity as in adversity, and to look not at its material but at virtue itself. And so neither poverty nor pain nor anything else that turns the inexperienced aside and drives them headlong stops him. Do you think him pressed by evils? He makes use of them. Not out of ivory alone did Phidias know how to make statues; he made them out of bronze. If you had offered him marble, if you had offered him even a cheaper material, he would have made out of it the best that could be made from it.

'Poverty is named not by possession, but by removal, or, as the ancients said, by deprivation. The Greeks call it kata steresin. It says not what a man has, but what he does not have. And so nothing can be filled up from many empty things. Riches are made up of many things, not of many instances of want. You understand poverty,' he says, 'otherwise than you ought. For poverty is not that which possesses few things, but that which does not possess many; thus it is named not from what it has, but from what is lacking to it.'

Is it so? Shall I unroll the annals of all the nations and ask who first wrote poems? Shall I, since I have no calendar, compute how much time lies between Orpheus and Homer? And shall I review the trifles of Aristarchus, with which he pricked the poems of others, and waste my years on syllables? Shall I so stick fast in the dust of geometry? Has that saving precept so slipped from me, 'Spare your time'? Shall I know these things? And what shall I not know?

And so, though now it tries to make good its loss, though it adds field to field, driving out a neighbour either by money or by wrong, though it extends its country estates to the size of provinces and calls a long journey through its own land a possession, no enlarging of bounds will bring us back to that from which we set out. When we have done all, we shall have much; we once had the whole.

Neither does philosophy; and yet it is not therefore useless and ineffective for the shaping of minds. What then? Is philosophy not the law of life? But let us grant that laws do not profit; it does not therefore follow that admonitions do not profit. Or by this reasoning deny that consolations profit, and dissuasions, and exhortations, and reproaches, and praises. All these are kinds of admonition. Through these one comes to the perfect state of the mind.

Let us suppose that someone does what he ought; he will not do it steadily, he will not do it evenly: for he will not know why he does it. Some things will come out right either by chance or by practice, but there will not be in his hand the rule by which they may be tested, by which he may believe that the things he has done are right. He will not promise himself that he will be such forever, who is good by chance.

"There is no doubt," he says, "that a peace never assailed is happier than one restored with much blood. There is no doubt that unshaken health is a happier thing than that which is brought to safety, out of grave diseases threatening the worst, by a certain force and endurance. In the same way there will be no doubt that joy is a greater good than a mind braced to endure the torments of wounds or of fire."

So the wise man will unfold his virtue, if he be allowed, amid riches, if not, amid poverty; if he can, in his country, if not, in exile; if he can, as a general, if not, as a soldier; if he can, whole, if not, maimed. Whatever fortune he has received, he will make of it something memorable.

I could express what I mean more easily if there were a Latin word by which what the Greeks call anyparxia, non-existence, were signified. This Antipater assigns to poverty; I do not see what poverty is other than the possession of little. We shall look into this, when at some time we are very much at leisure, what is the substance of riches, what of poverty; but then too we shall consider whether it is not better to soothe poverty and to take down the haughtiness of riches than to wrangle about words, as though the matter had already been judged.

The grammarian Apion, who went about all Greece in the days of Gaius Caesar and was adopted into the name of Homer by all the cities, used to say that Homer, when he had finished both his works, the Iliad and the Odyssey, added a beginning to his poem, in which he embraced the whole Trojan war. As proof of this argument he alleged that Homer had set in his first verse two letters by design, containing the number of his books.

The earth itself was more fertile when untilled, and bountiful for the uses of peoples who did not plunder it. Whatever nature had brought forth, it was no less a pleasure to have found than to show another what was found. Nor could anyone have either too much or too little; among men of one accord it was divided. Not yet had the stronger laid his hand upon the weaker, not yet had the greedy man, by hiding away what lay idle for himself, shut out another even from necessaries; each cared for the other as for himself.

Nothing more clothes minds with honour, and recalls the doubtful and those inclining to depravity to the right, than the company of good men. For little by little it sinks into the breast, and to be often looked upon, often heard, has the force of precepts. The mere meeting with the wise, by Hercules, profits, and there is something that flows from a great man even when he is silent.

Posidonius judges necessary not only prescription, for nothing forbids us to use this word, but also persuasion, consolation, and exhortation. To these he adds the inquiry into causes, aetiologia, which I do not see why we should not dare to call so, since the grammarians, the guardians of the Latin tongue, call it so by their own right. He says that the description of each virtue will also be useful; this Posidonius calls ethologia, some call it characterismos, rendering the signs and marks of each virtue and vice, by which things alike are distinguished among themselves.

What, do you think that Gaius Marius, once consul, for he received one consulship, the rest he snatched, when he was cutting down the Teutones and Cimbri, when he was pursuing Jugurtha through the deserts of Africa, sought so many perils at the prompting of virtue? Marius led the armies, ambition led Marius.

This thing has the same force as prescribing. For he who prescribes says: 'If you wish to be temperate, do thus.' He who describes says: 'He is temperate who does those things, who abstains from those.' Do you ask what the difference is? The one gives the precepts of virtue, the other its model. These descriptions and, to use the publicans' word, these likenesses, I confess, have their use; set the praiseworthy thing before us, and there will be one to imitate it.

These men, while they shook all things, were themselves shaken, after the manner of whirlwinds, which whirl about what they snatch up, but are themselves first whirled, and for this reason rush on with greater force, because they have no governance of themselves; and so, when they have been an evil to many, they themselves too feel that pestilent force by which they have harmed most men. There is no reason why you should believe that anyone becomes happy by another's unhappiness.

Do you think it useful that arguments be given you by which you may recognize a noble horse, lest you be deceived in buying, lest you waste your effort on a sluggish one? How much more useful is this, to know the marks of an excellent mind, which one is permitted to transfer from another into oneself!

All those examples, which are pressed upon our eyes and ears, must be unwoven, and the breast filled with evil speech must be emptied. Virtue must be brought into the occupied place, which may root out lies and the things that please contrary to truth, which may separate us from the people, whom we trust too much, and give us back to sincere opinions. For this is wisdom, to be turned back to nature and restored to that place from which the common error has driven us out.

'Straightway the foal of a noble stock steps higher in the fields and sets down his supple legs; first he dares both to go the road and to try the threatening rivers and to commit himself to an unknown bridge, nor does he shudder at empty noises. High is his neck and clean-cut his head, short his belly and full his back, and his spirited breast riots with muscles. Then, if from afar arms have given any sound, he knows not how to stand still, he pricks his ears and trembles in his limbs, and rolls under his nostrils the gathered fire.'

A great part of soundness is to have left behind the encouragers of madness and to have gone far from that mutually harmful gathering. That you may know this is true, look how differently each man lives for the people and for himself. Solitude is not of itself a teacher of innocence, nor do the fields teach frugality, but when the witness and spectator has withdrawn, the vices subside, whose fruit is to be displayed and beheld.

While doing something else, our Virgil has described a brave man; I, at least, would give no other image to a great man. If Marcus Cato were to be portrayed for me, set in the midst of the crashes of civil war, the first to defend the passes of the Alps, to throw himself in the way of war drawn down from Germany, I would give no other countenance.

Who puts on purple that he is to show to no one? Who lays out a feast in secret on gold? Who, flung beneath the shade of some rustic tree, unfolds alone the pomp of his luxury? No one is fine for his own eyes, nor even for those of a few or of his household, but spreads out the apparatus of his vices in proportion to the crowd that looks on.

Certainly no one could step higher than he who at once raised himself against both Caesar and Pompey, and, while some favoured Caesar's cause, others Pompey's, challenged both alike, and gave his vote to the commonwealth. For of Cato it is no less true: 'nor does he shudder at empty noises.' Why should he? When he was not shaken even by true ones.

So it is: the admirer and the witness is the incitement of all the things over which we are mad. You will bring it about that we do not covet, if you bring it about that we do not display. Ambition and luxury and ungovernableness need a stage: you will cure these things if you hide them.

How great is the vigour and spirit in him, how great the confidence in the public trembling! He knows that he is the one man whose standing is not at stake; for the question is not whether Cato is free, but whether he is among the free; thence his contempt of perils and swords. It is a joy to apply to that man's indomitable steadfastness those words: 'his spirited breast riots with muscles.'

And so, if we are placed in the midst of the uproar of cities, let a monitor stand at our side and, against those who praise vast estates, let him praise the man rich on little and measuring wealth by use. Against those who exalt influence and power, let him himself look up to the leisure handed over to letters and to a mind turned back from externals to its own.

It will profit not only to say of what sort good men are wont to be, and to draw out their form and lineaments, but to relate and set forth of what sort they have been: Cato's last and bravest wound, through which he let out his freedom; the wisdom of Laelius and his concord with his friend Scipio; the noble deeds of the elder Cato at home and abroad; the wooden couches of Tubero, spread for a public banquet, and the goat-skins instead of coverlets, and, before the very shrine of Jupiter, earthen vessels set out for the feast. What else was this than to consecrate poverty on the Capitol? Though I have no other deed of his by which to enrol him among the Catos, do we think this too little? It was a censorship, not a dinner.

Let him show that those happy by the world's reckoning are, on that envied pinnacle of theirs, trembling and stunned, and holding a far different opinion of themselves than is held by others. For the things that seem lofty to others are, to themselves, sheer precipices. And so they are breathless and tremble as often as they have looked down on that precipice of their own greatness. For they think on the various mishaps, and on heights especially slippery.

Oh, how ignorant are men greedy of glory, what it is or how it must be sought! On that day the Roman people beheld the furniture of many, admired that of one. The gold and silver of all those others has been broken up and melted down a thousand times over; but to all ages the goat-skins of Tubero will be famous. Farewell.

Then they dread the things they sought, and happiness, which makes them burdensome to others, lies the more heavily upon themselves. Then they praise leisure, gentle and in one's own power; brightness is hateful, and flight from things still standing is sought. Then at last you may see men philosophizing through fear, and taking good counsel through their evils. For, as though these things were contrary to each other, good fortune and a good mind, so we grow wiser in evils; prosperity takes away the right. Farewell.
